name: Kids agent (waits for a local model): text with homework hints, chat hours, parent alerts and a nightly digest, then the kitchen speaker
description: Later, each child texts Happy from their own Apple account and gets a helper with no tools and no memory, on a local model, that gives grade-level hints and short explanations and is told not to hand over a finished worksheet; the parents get chat hours per child, an immediate text when a message is flagged for safety or distress, and an evening digest of what each child asked. As a second step the same kids agent answers by voice through the roadmap's kitchen speaker (Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition), with wake word, speech-to-text and text-to-speech running locally so that only text reaches Happy.
example: Trigger: at 21:40 the 8-year-old texts the kids agent and gets a fixed 'time for bed, ask me tomorrow' line. At the kitchen speaker: 'Okay Nabu, why is the sky blue?'
how: Base (F072): `bindings[]` by DM handle to one agent per kid, the minimal profile with `session_status` and `gateway` denied, memory search off, a daily reset and an in-house kid-safety plugin with a local classifier on `before_dispatch` and `message_sending`. Hints (F073): hint-first rules and a grade band in AGENTS.md; no URLs. Hours and alerts (MKT-13): the same plugin gives a fixed reply outside each kid's hours and texts both parents the category and time on a safety label. Digest (G019): a host-side command job summarises the day's sessions on a local model. Speaker (VOX-11): the device, Home Assistant OS in a VM on the Mac, Whisper and Piper through the Wyoming integration, and a kids-only shim in front of the gateway, whose OpenAI-compatible chat endpoint is full operator access.
caveats: Blocked until a local model and local classifiers exist and the kid-safety evals pass, because kids' content never goes to a cloud model or cloud speech.

A local classifier's accuracy on how 8 and 10-year-olds actually write is unproven: false alarms will annoy, misses matter more, and a home system has no human reviewer between the flag and the parent notice.

Common Sense Media rated Google's supervised assistant for under-13s high risk and recommends that children aged 6 to 12 use chatbots only under adult supervision; an alert and an evening digest are a look afterwards, not supervision, so whether a child may chat alone is a decision to take before building.
'Refuse whole-worksheet answers' is a prompt rule, and no source shows a model holds to it when a child pushes.
The alert is a heads-up to parents and not a crisis service, and the parents should be told so.

The speaker has no interim adult version: nothing identifies who is speaking, so without a local model a child's question would reach OpenAI as text, and speech stays in the house only while Home Assistant's own cloud speech option is left off.

The hop from Home Assistant to Happy is unsolved: Home Assistant's official OpenAI integration only talks to OpenAI's own endpoint, and with token auth OpenClaw's chat endpoint gives the caller the full operator scope set and lets the request choose the agent, so the bridge would be a community integration or a self-written kids-only shim.

The speaker adds an always-on VM to patch and back up, Home Assistant itself calls the device a preview, and open-ended questions need Whisper, which Home Assistant recommends only on powerful hardware.
How the safety plugin texts the parents from inside a hook is not settled: no plugin-side send path was found in the hook docs read, so an 'immediate' alert is the aim, not a tested behaviour.
corrections: 'OpenAI terms are 13+, no cloud shortcut' could not be confirmed as worded: OpenAI's consumer Terms of Use returned HTTP 403 in this run, and the API page that did open sets no flat 13+ bar. It says personal data of children under 13 must not be processed without zero data retention and that COPPA applies. Keeping kids off the cloud stays the family's rule; store:false was not shown to count as zero data retention.
unverified: Llama Guard 3 as the classifier is the roadmap's choice and appears nowhere in the installed OpenClaw docs (its Ollama library page is cited under G019).
Whether kids admitted by pairing are refused as approvers; the roadmap itself marks this as untested.
How accurate any local classifier is on questions from 8 and 10 year olds; no evaluation exists yet.
'Refuse whole-worksheet answers' is a prompt rule; no source shows a model holds to it when a child pushes.
A parent asking the same questions from their own chat works today, but that is the parent using the cloud model, not the child.
Whether the Apple on-device model can be called from a host job for an ad hoc summary; the doc gives it an 8,192-token window and 1,024 output tokens and describes utility use only.
Reading the per-agent database from a command job (read-only open or the history RPC) was not tried.

Which session transcript a delivered digest line is copied into: the installed source appends direct scheduled deliveries to a session transcript (dist/delivery-dispatch-awareness-CcGkYFaV.mjs:518), and if that session belongs to a parent's cloud-backed agent, the quoted kid text would reach a cloud model.
Whether ChatGPT's controls changed after the September 2025 launch report; OpenAI's own page returned 403 in this run.
How the plugin sends a proactive message to the parents from inside a hook; G009 covers the agent `message` tool and host jobs, and no plugin-side send path was found in the hook docs read.
Which Home Assistant conversation integration can target a custom OpenAI-compatible endpoint in 2026 (the roadmap cites a community one; I did not verify it).
Whisper latency inside a VM on this Mac.
Whether OpenClaw can issue an HTTP credential scoped to one agent.

Whether a trusted-proxy identity in front of the HTTP endpoint could narrow a caller to one agent. With the token auth this gateway uses, the docs say scope headers are ignored and the request's model field selects any agent.
safety: The design keeps the children's content off the cloud: the agent, its classifiers and the digest summariser are local, and with the classifier down the agent answers 'ask a grown-up'. Alerts carry a category, not the child's words. Two points are open. The nightly digest tells the parents what a child asked and is delivered into a parent's chat with Happy; OpenClaw copies a scheduled delivery into a session transcript, and if that session belongs to a parent's cloud-backed agent the child's words would reach the cloud model, so the delivery route has to be checked before the digest quotes anything. And the speaker's bridge: the chat endpoint is equivalent to an operator secret, so the speaker must reach only the tool-less kids agent.

name: Scheduled-jobs registry in family.json5: per-person switches, a charter per job, failure guardrails
description: Every scheduled feature becomes a named switch per person in one reviewed file. From that entry the generator creates the job with a time limit and a tool cap and writes a short charter the parents can read: what Happy may do without asking, what needs a yes first, when to stop and ask, what it must never do. Failure alerts are routed to Tony instead of the family; a job that keeps failing stops itself, and whether that last notice reaches Tony or the job owner's thread is still to be checked; recurring runs missed during a power cut are skipped, while one-off reminders still catch up.
example: Turning Jordan's school digest off is a one-line change Tony reviews. The 19:30 brief fails twice in a row: Tony gets one text, and one more when it recovers. After a power cut the 07:00 brief does not turn up at 11:40.
how: gen-family reads the family.json5 flags and emits `openclaw automations add/edit/remove`, keyed on the stable `--name`, with `--agent`, `--to`, `--tz`, `--announce`, `--timeout-seconds` and an explicit `--tools` cap on every job; it diffs against `automations list --all --json`, because the default list hides disabled jobs. The same entries render one `## Program: <name>` section per job (Authority, Trigger, Approval gate, Escalation, What NOT to do, plus an execute-verify-report rule) into templates/person/AGENTS.md, and each job message points at its program instead of repeating it; isolated jobs must not use `--light-context`, which drops the bootstrap files. Gateway config: a global `cron.failureAlert` object routed to the operator's handle; `cron.skipMissedJobs: true`; `cron.triggers.enabled: false`. These three switches are plain config and can go in before the generator exists; triggers must be off before timed reminders (F007) or any other item gives an agent the `automations` tool. happy-inspect reads `automations list --all` to catch auto-disabled jobs. The healthchecks dead-man switch stays the only signal for a Mac that is off.
caveats: A charter is prompt text, not enforcement; the hard limits stay in tool policy and hooks.

AGENTS.md shares a bootstrap budget (20,000 characters per file by default); keep each program to about ten lines. Scheduled runs do not get MEMORY.md, so anything a program needs must be in AGENTS.md, the job message or a tool result.
A chat instruction does not change a charter; it waits for a reviewed deploy.
By default a failure alert goes to the failing job's own announce target, so Jordan would get 'job failed' texts for her jobs unless they are rerouted to Tony.
Alerts start after 2 failures in a row with a 1-hour cooldown. A recurring job is switched off after 10 failures in a row and then disappears from the default job list.
Without a per-job timeout an isolated agent job is bounded only by a 60-minute watchdog.
After a reboot with FileVault locked nothing fires and nothing alerts. One-shot reminders still catch up after an outage even with skipMissedJobs set.

Jobs an agent creates in chat, once

-main holds the automations tool, are outside the registry, so the diff must tolerate or report them.

With triggers on, trigger scripts and script payloads run with the owning agent's full tool policy, exec included. Switching triggers off also switches off the trigger-script design of F029 until that is deliberately turned back on.
corrections: Diffing against 'automations list --json' is not enough: the list shows enabled jobs only unless --all is passed, so a job disabled by a mute would look missing and be created twice. Use 'automations list --all --json'.
unverified: Whether gen-family, run from Tony's admin account, can reach the happy user's Gateway with the admin operator scope the docs require.
Whether scheduler-sent failure alerts pass through the G009 recipient-pin hook or bypass it.
Where the auto-disable notice lands: the docs say the owning agent receives it even when failure alerts are off, so it may reach the family member's thread instead of Tony's.
safety: Purely restrictive. Charters narrow behaviour and grant nothing; never-list items are written under What NOT to do and are also unreachable by tool policy. Alert text shown in chat is a normalized cause, and routing alerts to the operator keeps one person's job details out of another person's thread.

name: Stop by text: 'Happy, stop everything', and lock one person out
description: Either parent can text one exact phrase and Happy stops: no agent runs and no tool calls until Tony switches it back on at the Mac. Texts from scheduled jobs that use no model (the weather and page watchers) are cancelled only on a best-effort basis until Tony also switches the scheduler off. A second phrase stops Happy answering one person's handle, for a lost or stolen phone.
example: Jordan texts 'Happy, stop everything' when briefs start arriving twice. Tony texts 'Happy, lock out Jordan' after her phone is left in a taxi.
how: In-house plugin. before_dispatch claims the exact phrase from an adult's handle and writes a kill file (everything) or a suspended file (one person's handles). The stop is enforced where hooks fail closed: before_agent_run blocks agent runs before the model reads the prompt, and before_tool_call blocks tools; message_sending cancels scheduled announce texts as a best-effort extra. Levels that need no plugin code, done by Tony: `cron.enabled: false`, then `openclaw gateway stop`. Lifting a stop or a lock-out is CLI-only. For a stolen phone the operator step still has to follow: remove the handle from family.json5 and redeploy, which is the only thing that ends that handle's approver rights; `openclaw devices revoke` if the phone ran the OpenClaw app; Find My Lost Mode on the phone side.
caveats: The phrase matcher is a claim hook and message_sending is a delivery hook: both log and continue when their handler throws or times out, so the stop must not live only there.
Command jobs make no agent run, so their announce texts can only be caught by message_sending (as read from the bundled code, not yet tested); the dependable stop for those is the scheduler switch.
/stop (OCL-06) ends one answer in one chat; this stops everything.
For a stolen phone, 'stop everything' already works as the blunt version; the lock-out phrase only keeps Happy answering the other parent in the meantime.
A locked phone already stops most misuse. The lock-out covers a phone taken while unlocked or a passcode seen over a shoulder.
Either adult can lock the other out, and Tony undoes it at the Mac. If whoever holds the phone sends the phrase first, the real owner needs the CLI.
A lock-out stops replies and texts to that person, not their scheduled jobs; pause those too with the mute and vacation controls in G001.
Keep both phrases out of Happy's own help text and replies.

The fixed emergency reply (CRT-13) is planned as a second phrase list in this same plugin. It must keep answering while Happy is stopped or a person is locked out, so whatever cancels outgoing texts during a stop or a lock-out has to let that one fixed line through.
corrections: 'Freeze every outbound write' is fail-closed only for tool calls. The phrase matcher and the message_sending check both log and continue when their handler throws or times out, so a broken plugin lets the phrase reach the model and lets scheduled announce texts out. The levels that do not depend on plugin code are the scheduler switch and stopping the Gateway.
unverified: That before_agent_run fires for scheduled agent-turn jobs on this build; test with a throwaway job.
Whether switching the scheduler off stops a job already running, and whether switching it back needs a restart (the hot-reload table says no; the automation troubleshooting page says restart).
How plugin code running as the happy user would change the scheduler setting, given the config repo is read-only to it; the kill file may be the only chat-triggered level.
What the sender sees when before_agent_run blocks a run and no replacement message is set.
Whether a tapback from a suspended handle can still resolve a pending approval, and whether owner-only slash commands from that handle are parsed before the plugin's hooks run.

The Shortcut and ntfy-button triggers from the 9 Oct entry: where an ntfy action request originates, and whether it can reach the Gateway over Tailscale, was not confirmed, so the text phrase is the only confirmed trigger.
safety: Both phrases can only narrow what Happy does; nothing in the chat path can add a sender or switch anything back on. A chat lock-out leaves the handle on channels.imessage.allowFrom, which is also the approver list, so that person's agent runs and tool calls must be blocked by the fail-closed hooks until Tony removes the handle and redeploys.

name: When the model is down: an honest notice, jobs that need no model, and an optional same-vendor fallback
description: When the cloud model has an incident, a parent who texts Happy today gets OpenClaw's own error line, which may be little more than the provider's status (its exact wording on iMessage has not been seen), and a scheduled brief is simply missed: the scheduler's own failure notice starts only after two failures in a row, and the jobs registry (G003) routes it to Tony, not the family. With this, when model errors go on for a set number of minutes, each parent gets one plain 'the model is down' line and later a 'back' line, and the alerts that need no model keep working: the weather watch, the stop phrase, and any fixed reminder Tony has set up as a no-model job (bin day). As an option Tony has to decide on, the vendor's lower-cost model answers that turn and the chat shows a one-line notice saying so; OpenClaw's security guidance warns against running an agent that has tools on a smaller model, so this part stays off unless he accepts that.
example: Trigger: gpt-6-sol returns server errors at 07:00 while the morning brief is due, and the error alert stays on past the set number of minutes. Each parent gets one fixed line saying the model is down and that weather alerts and fixed reminders still arrive, and one 'back' line once it recovers; the 07:00 brief itself is missed.
how:
Today each person agent is generated with `model.fallbacks: []`, and the docs say an agent's primary is strict unless its model object lists fallbacks, so after the built-in retries a failure surfaces as a terminal error that keeps the provider's HTTP status. Three steps. (1) Fallback (optional; it needs Tony's decision, because OpenClaw's prompt-injection guidance says not to run tool-enabled agents on smaller model tiers): add gpt-6-luna on the same per-person provider id as the single fallback for

-main, one line in gen-family, since both models are already in that agent's modelPolicy.allow under the same key and store setting. The docs say a fallback is used for that turn only and a one-line notice is shown in direct chats. Mail and kid agents keep `fallbacks: []` as the roadmap requires. This covers model-scoped incidents and rate limits, not a vendor-wide outage. (2) Model-free jobs: the weather watch (F018) is specified as a `--command-argv` job and the stop phrase (G005) is a `before_dispatch` claim, so both work through an outage. Timed reminders (F007) and the briefs are `--message` jobs, which the docs define as model-backed agent turns, so they fail with the model; a fixed-text reminder that must not be missed, such as bin day, has to be created as a command job that prints its line. A scheduled agent turn can also carry its own `--fallbacks` list. (3) Outage notice: extend the health watch (G008) so that when the existing error-ratio alert has fired for N minutes, a host script sends each parent one fixed line and later one 'back' line by a model-free send: `openclaw message send` to the pinned family handles, or a command job with announce delivery. The catalog's usual host path, `openclaw agent --deliver`, runs an agent turn and so cannot announce a model outage. `openclaw models status --check` is not the detector: its own docs say a clean exit does not prove a request will succeed.
depends_on: decision: whether the vendor's lower-cost model may answer for a parent's main agent when the usual one fails, against OpenClaw's guidance not to run tool-enabled agents on smaller models (the notice and the no-model jobs do not wait on this)
G008 health watch and the O1 error-ratio alert
G009 family delivery (for the notice)
caveats: OpenClaw's prompt-injection guidance says not to use smaller or cheaper model tiers for agents that have tools or read outside content, and each parent's main agent does both (reminders, lists, family delivery, photos and PDFs). The fallback here is the vendor's lower-cost model, so allowing it is a decision and not a default; without it an outage means the plain notice and no answers until the usual model is back.

OpenAI's status history listed 39 incidents in September 2026 and 23 in the first ten days of October across all its products. Most do not touch the API models Happy uses, but some did, for example 'elevated error rates across API models' on 17 Sep.
An answer from the smaller model can be worse than the usual one; the fallback notice tells the parent which model answered.
No fallback to a second vendor: it would need another vendor's key and a new privacy decision, and the local route is the skipped M2, so a vendor-wide outage still means no answers until it ends.
An API key that hits its monthly cap looks like an outage until the month ends; the fixed line should say 'limit reached' when that is the cause.
If the Mac, the home internet or iMessage is what failed, nothing here helps. The dead-man alert is then the only signal and it goes to Tony.

A scheduled brief that fails is simply missed unless the job's retry settings say otherwise. OpenClaw's scheduler already sends a failure notice after two failures in a row and one recovery notice afterwards, but the jobs registry (G003) routes those to Tony, so the line built here is the only word the family gets.

A parent who texts during an outage is not met with silence today: the failover page says that when every model fails the failure is shown, and that the reply can be a more specific line, such as one saying all models are temporarily rate-limited, with the time the cooldown ends when that is known. What this card adds is the unprompted line to both parents and the 'back' line.
safety: No new data path. The fallback uses the same provider id, key and store:false setting, and the notice is a fixed string to pinned family recipients. Mail and kid agents stay strict, so their content can never move to another model by accident.
unverified: The exact text a parent sees on iMessage when every candidate fails; the docs describe it, it was not triggered in this run.
Whether gpt-6-luna stays healthy during typical gpt-6-sol incidents.
Whether command jobs deliver normally while model calls are failing; nothing suggests otherwise but it was not tested.
Whether 'openclaw message send' passes through the same recipient-pinning hook as the agent's message tool; if it does not, the host script must hard-code the family handles from the registry.

name: Notification policy: daily cap, quiet hours, priority classes and job tags, plus snooze, mute and vacation mode by chat
description: Caps how many unprompted texts each parent gets in a day, stops non-urgent ones outside allowed hours and labels each one so you know which job sent it. A text stopped by the cap or the hours is dropped, not sent later, so scheduled jobs are timed inside the allowed hours in the first place. Either parent can text 'mute until 3' or 'we are away next week', and briefs, bin reminders and routines pause for that window while urgent alerts still arrive. The pause is dependable only for a job that holds the household-store tool and checks the pause itself (the week-ahead and morning briefs as specified, and the evening brief once it is given that read), and best effort for timed reminders and any other job without the tool, which can only be stopped at delivery.
example: Jordan texts: 'We are away next week.' Briefs and bin reminders stop for the week; an urgent alert still arrives.
how: Policy (G001): an in-house plugin with `before_tool_call` on `message` (fails closed) and a `message_sending` cancel for `--announce` deliveries (fails open on error); counters live in the household store, and schedules are generated inside the allowed windows in the first place. Pause (G002): a paused-until row in the same store. A job that holds the store tool reads the row first and answers `NO_REPLY`. A job that cannot read it, such as a timed reminder, which runs with an empty tool list (F007), is paused by the plugin's delivery hook instead: the hook reads the same row and cancels the text. For a long absence a host helper can also run `openclaw automations disable|enable <job-id>`, and `cron.enabled: false` pauses everything. The policy's priority classes decide which alerts still pass during a mute. OpenClaw also lets a command owner (a sender listed in `commands.ownerAllowFrom`) ask the agent to change an existing automation by chat; that is not the route used here (see caveats).
caveats: Each iPhone can already silence the night on a schedule, so what Happy adds is the daily cap, the urgent or not-urgent split, the label and the pause by chat.

The delivery hook can only rewrite or cancel a text, so one stopped by the daily cap or by quiet hours is dropped, not delivered later; holding texts and releasing them in a batch would need a queue of the plugin's own, which is not designed. Scheduled jobs are therefore timed inside the allowed hours, and the hook is the backstop.

It is not a hard gate for scheduled texts: the message_sending hook that sees `--announce` deliveries lets the message through if the plugin throws or times out, and only the agent's own message tool is gated fail-closed.
The reading of the announce path comes from bundled JavaScript and not a doc page, so confirm it with a throwaway hook before relying on either hook.
No doc lists a job id on message_sending, so each job may have to write its own tag into the text.
No built-in quiet hours or priority classes were found in OpenClaw, so keeping urgent alerts on during a mute depends on this plugin.
The household store does not exist yet, so the counters and the paused-until row are a design and not an installed feature.
The fixed emergency reply (CRT-13) answers an inbound text and must never be held back by quiet hours, caps or a mute.

Timed reminders run with an empty tool list (F007), so a reminder job cannot check the pause itself; its text is stopped only by the delivery hook, which is the best-effort side. A mute is therefore dependable only for jobs that hold the household-store tool and read the row themselves, and best effort for reminders. Because a stopped text is dropped and not sent late, a one-off reminder that falls inside a mute would be lost, so one-off reminders a parent set belong in a class that passes; a recurring one such as the bins reminder can pause, because the next one comes round anyway.

Switching a job off by chat is open only to a command owner, which is Tony's handle alone today (adding Jordan is the open decision recorded on F007). OpenClaw's page gives that sender's agent the power to update, run or remove any job on the Gateway, not only to pause one, and a job changed that way no longer matches the registry (G003). The paused-until row is the route both parents use, and it changes no job.

The evening brief (F014) is specified with the weather and calendar tools only, so as written it cannot read the paused-until row. Give that job the household-store read as well, or its pause rests on the best-effort delivery hook, like a timed reminder's.
corrections: reply_payload_sending does not cover --announce on the installed build: the scheduler's announce path sends without a reply-payload hook descriptor and the outbound stage skips that hook when none is supplied. message_sending is the hook that sees those deliveries (the G005 wording already uses it), and it fails open on handler error, so it is a best-effort gate.

The 9 Oct note said switching jobs off needs operator.admin and so cannot be done from

-main; the installed docs also let a sender listed in `commands.ownerAllowFrom` ask the agent to disable an existing automation by chat.
unverified: The announce-path reading comes from bundled JavaScript, not a doc page; confirm with a throwaway hook before relying on either hook.
How the hook learns which job produced a text; no doc lists a job id on message_sending, so the job may have to write its own tag into the text.
Whether a scheduled iPhone Do Not Disturb can silence only Happy's thread; Apple's page confirmed scheduling and allowed people, not per-contact silencing.
The home-store plugin does not exist yet; the paused-until row is a design, not an installed feature.
safety: Both halves only hold back or pause Happy's own unprompted texts; neither adds a recipient, a tool or a data source. Urgent classes keep passing during a mute, and switching everything off stays an operator action.

name: Weather tool upgrade: hourly rain and snow, and alert details, from the National Weather Service
description: Ask about rain during Saturday's game or active weather alerts for home, with hour-by-hour detail and snowfall, straight from the National Weather Service.
example: Jordan texts: 'Will it rain during Saturday's 10 o'clock game?' Happy answers with the hourly chance of rain from 9 to noon and any active alert for home.
how: Extend the in-house home_weather plugin: follow forecastHourly from /points, add alert id, read snowfallAmount from the raw gridpoint endpoint; keep the api.weather.gov host pin.
caveats: Apple's Weather app can already send a notification when rain or snow is about to start or stop, and for government-issued severe-weather alerts at a saved location; Apple notes this is not offered in every country or region. This tool earns its place as the weather feed for the briefs (F014) and the trip planner (F028), which need an hourly rain window, and for questions asked inside a Happy conversation. The weather watch (F018) polls the alerts feed with its own script and does not depend on this tool.
The National Weather Service hourly forecast reaches seven days ahead, so a question about a game further out gets no hour-by-hour answer until the date comes into range.
unverified: The snowfall field name and units were seen only in the OpenAPI description of the raw gridpoint endpoint, not in a live response.
NWS publishes no numeric rate limit, so the 10-minute cache is a design choice rather than an NWS rule.
Whether those Weather notifications are offered and switched on for the home location on each parent's iPhone: the Apple page read was the Mac Weather guide, and the iPhone guide did not render.
safety: Read-only public data from one pinned government host. A lookup sends the home's coordinates and the header that identifies the app, as the National Weather Service asks, and nothing else about the family. The forecast and alert text that comes back is outside content, though from a single government source; the tool only reads, and it cannot write anything or message anyone.

name: School mailbox with an isolated reader and a weekday 16:00 digest
description: A separate mailbox registered with school, PTA, coaches and the lunch system is read by an isolated, memory-less reader, so no parent's private inbox is touched. Weekday afternoons both parents get a five-line text of the day's school and activity mail with dates spelled out, a dated to-do list, and one line per child from the school platforms' own summary emails where the school uses them. A parent who wants a day-before reminder for a line asks their own agent for it. Attachments are not opened: a newsletter sent as a PDF or a picture shows up only as a file name.
example: Trigger: weekdays at 16:00. Text: 'School mail today: picture day is Thursday 15 October, order form due Wednesday 14 October; PTA meeting moved to Tuesday 20 October at 7 pm; lunch balance is low.' Jordan then texts Happy: 'remind me Tuesday evening about the picture day form.'
how: Mailbox (F051): the bundled `imap` plugin on a new mailbox (iCloud needs `watch.mode: "interval"`), a sender allowlist that includes both parents for forwards, and a tool-less reader. With the plugin's `deliver` switch off, which is the default, its per-message reader announces nothing, and the account settings name no recipient, so reaching the parents needs a hook-pinned `message` tool or a scheduled sweep. Digest (F056): `automations create '0 16 * * 1-5' --agent school-mail --session isolated --announce --to <chat>` with `--tools school-mail-ro__*`; the read MCP is `gog mcp` (Gmail) or a himalaya wrapper (iCloud). Setup done once by a parent, per platform: ParentSquare posts set to Digest with email on, PowerSchool's scheduled emails and Balance Alert sent to the mailbox, Google Classroom guardian summaries, the lunch service's low-balance alert, library notices; each sender goes on the allowlist.
caveats: Pick the mailbox provider with the password in mind: the plugin signs in with a mailbox password only, which on Gmail means a Google app password that Google does not recommend, while OpenClaw's guide names Fastmail and iCloud.

Each school system has to accept an extra guardian address, a manual chore per system, and auto-forwarding from a parent's Gmail may fail the plugin's aligned-DMARC check, so registering the address directly is the safe route.
The reader gets body text and attachment file names only, so PDF or image newsletters and flyer attachments are not read.

Urgent alerts are not this digest's job, since the school's own alerts reach the parents' phones first; the reader keeps one backup rule (a closure, delay or early-dismissal message from an allowlisted school sender is passed on at the next sweep, not held until 16:00), and sorting urgent from routine on real district mail is untested.

PowerSchool emails carry grades and attendance and Classroom summaries carry assignment titles: these are a child's education records and they reach the cloud model under store:false, which is why the card is rated medium risk.
Classroom summaries (missing and upcoming work, no grades) arrive only if the school uses Classroom and the teacher switches them on, and the guardian invitation expires after 120 days.
One job appears to take one delivery target, so two parents need two jobs or the parents' group chat, and the iCloud read path likely needs an in-house himalaya wrapper.

For a school or team app that sends no email, try the app's own email notifications into this mailbox first and a parent's screenshot to Happy second; Canvas and ClassDojo have no verified email path.

The reminder step is not wired end to end. The reader that writes the digest holds no reminder or store tool, on purpose, because it reads untrusted mail, and it is untested whether the parent's own agent, which receives any reply, can see the digest text. Until that is tested, a parent names the line when asking their own agent for a reminder. Giving the reader a write to the household store would let text from a school email reach the parents' private agents, so that route needs its own review first.

The sender list lives in family.json5 and changes only with a reviewed deploy, so a parent who needs a new coach or teacher added asks Tony. The mail plugin logs a rejected message without its subject or body, so a mail that did not show up can be traced in the gateway log.
A calendar link that a school platform offers is subscribed in the family calendar (F009), not read by this reader.

The sender check with verified authentication runs only on the mail plugin's per-message path. The 16:00 digest job reads the mailbox itself through the read-only mail tool, so mail from a sender who is not on the list (spam, a faked address) would reach the reader unless the job filters by sender or the digest is built only from what the plugin let in. The reader holds nothing but the mailbox read and can only text the two parents, which limits the harm to a misleading digest line. Which of the two routes builds the digest is not settled.
corrections: 'IMAP passes body text only' is slightly off: the plugin's prompt also lists attachment file names (dist/extensions/imap/index.js:55735). Contents of attached PDFs or images are still not passed, so flyer attachments remain unread.
'school-mail-ro MCP is gog (Gmail)' needs no wrapper code on the Gmail path: upstream gogcli ships a read-only stdio MCP server (`gog mcp`).
The built-in scheduling tool is listed as `automations`, with `cron` kept as an alias (docs/gateway/config-tools/tool-policy.md:73).
unverified: Whether the district, PTA, coaches and lunch system each accept an extra or shared guardian address; this is a manual chore per system.

Auto-forwarding school mail from a parent's Gmail by filter may fail the plugin's aligned-DMARC check (Google's forwarding guidance says forwarded mail often fails SPF); DKIM survival was not tested, so registering the address directly is the safe route.
An iCloud+ custom-domain address with this plugin was not tested; Apple documents the IMAP host and app-specific passwords, not this combination.

Whether himalaya has an MCP mode; its README does not mention one, so the iCloud path likely needs an in-house wrapper. The README also says native keyring support was removed in v2, so its password comes from a command.
That one job takes exactly one delivery target (hence two jobs or one group chat for two parents); I saw single-target examples only.
Groups are off today, so a family group chat target needs the iMessage group allowlist switched on first.
Which platforms this family's district uses, and each platform's exact sender address and authentication result.
Whether the school uses Google Classroom at all, and whether a student can have the school mailbox as an extra guardian next to both parents.
ClassDojo's notification behaviour and Canvas's calendar feed for observers; neither page could be opened.
Whether a parent's reply to the digest reaches an agent that can see the digest text: the digest is announced by the school-mail agent from an isolated run, and replies go to the parent's own agent.

What the mail plugin's `deliver` switch does when it is on: the account settings have the switch (off by default) but no recipient field, so where a reader's summary would go is not documented on the page read.
safety: All school mail is untrusted and is read only by the memory-less school-mail agent, which has no web or file tools and can only announce to the two parents. The sender allowlist with verified authentication is the mail plugin's check on its own per-message path; the 16:00 digest job reads the mailbox through a separate read-only tool that this check does not cover, so that job needs its own sender filter (see caveats). Links are relayed only when their domain matches the allowlisted sender. No agent logs in to a school portal and no portal credentials are stored.

name: Childcare coverage planner: no-school days and summer weeks
description: A grid of every weekday the kids have no school (teacher days, breaks, early releases, the ten or so summer weeks) against who covers it: camp, grandparents, a trip, a parent off work. Happy keeps the grid, lists the open cells months ahead, reminds the parents of the registration dates they give it (with a page watch for a camp whose site can be read), and at tax time lists what was paid to which day camp from the receipts a parent sent. School and camp form paperwork is a separate entry (CRT-12).
example: Trigger: first Sunday of February. Happy texts both parents: 'Jordan coverage: 4 of 10 weeks open for the 10-year-old, 6 for the 8-year-old. Two camps you saved open registration this week.'
how:
Inputs: the district calendar (a public feed the family Google Calendar is subscribed to, read through F009, or a photo or PDF through the dates-after-a-yes flow, F010) gives the no-school weekdays; parents add coverage by text. Store: household store rows (F031) keyed by date range and child nickname, with a status (open, pencilled, booked, paid) and a provider name. Jobs: a monthly isolated job on

-main from January to May, and weekly in the four weeks before each break ('--cron'), listing open cells; page watchers for 'registration opens' on camps the parents name (the changed-page watch in F018, created by Tony); options research by the stateless research agent given ages, weeks and a distance only (F019). Parents register and pay themselves. After paying, a parent sends the receipt and Happy records amount and provider. In February it lists day-camp totals per provider and which providers still lack a taxpayer number, because IRS Publication 503 treats day camp, and not overnight camp, as a possible work-related care expense for a child under 13, and asks for the provider's name, address and taxpayer number (Form W-10 is the request form).
depends_on: F031 household store
F009 family calendar subscribed to the district feed, or F010 for a district calendar PDF
F018 page watchers and F019 research agent
F007 reminders
F002 photo and PDF reading, for receipts (its privacy gate screens text PDFs only)
caveats: Most states set the school year near 180 days (28 states in the NCES table), which leaves roughly 80 weekdays a year without school, holidays included. The planner earns its keep only if both parents work on those days.
Camp sites are often script-heavy or bot-walled. Expect 'could not verify' and rely on the parent pasting dates.
Registration is a booking and a payment. Happy stops at the reminder and the link.
The tax list is for the preparer, not tax advice. Whether a camp qualifies depends on facts Happy does not have.
A shared spreadsheet does the grid. The gain here is the reminders, the registration watch and the receipts list for tax time.
safety:
The grid lives with

-main, which holds private data and does not browse. The research agent gets ages, date ranges and distance only, never names, school or address. The page watchers are host scripts with no model (F018) and hold no private data. No registration, booking or payment is performed. A receipt sent as a photo is read by the cloud model like any other photo; the privacy gate in F002 screens text PDFs only.
unverified: Whether the family's district publishes a calendar feed or only a PDF.
That the 2025 edition of Publication 503 carries over unchanged to the 2026 tax year.

name: Family logistics briefs: evening (19:30), Sunday week-ahead (18:00), weekday morning (07:00)
description: Each parent gets short scheduled texts built from the family calendar and the weather. Sunday to Thursday at 19:30: tomorrow's events, who drives, what to pack and the weather, and nothing when the day is unremarkable. Sunday at 18:00: the week ahead, with early releases, activities, drivers, packing, the weather outlook and open school deadlines. Optionally, weekdays at 07:00: weather and alerts, today's calendar, items due and trash day. Mail stays in its own digests: the school digest (F051) and each parent's 07:00 mail digest (part of G015).
example: Sunday to Thursday at 19:30 each parent gets one text: tomorrow's two events and who drives each, 'pack shin guards', and rain after 3.
how:
One isolated job per parent per brief on

-main, all from one template: tools `home_weather` plus the read-only calendar MCP (`

-calendar__*`), no web tools, no `--light-context`, `--tz` set, `--announce --to imessage:`. Schedules: evening `--cron "30 19 * * 0-4"`, week-ahead `--cron "0 18 * * 0"`, morning `--cron "0 7 * * 1-5"`. The routines and gear table lives in AGENTS.md; a run replies `NO_REPLY` to stay silent. The week-ahead and morning legs also read the household store (F031) for items due, trash day and open school deadlines. Email-derived dates for the week-ahead come from a separate

-mail job using `llm-task`, never the same run. Build the evening brief first; the morning brief is the optional one.
caveats: On Sundays the 18:00 week-ahead and the 19:30 evening brief would both arrive within ninety minutes. Either let the Sunday week-ahead carry Monday's detail and run the evening brief Monday to Thursday only (`1-4`), or accept two texts.

The morning leg is the optional one: it needs the household store (F031) for items due and trash day, and the weather plugin returns no sunset, so a sunset line, if wanted, needs a small local calculation.

If the optional 07:00 morning brief and the morning mail digest (part of G015) are both switched on, a parent gets two texts at 07:00. They cannot be one job, because the mail agent and the parent's main agent are kept apart; move one of them by a quarter of an hour, or leave the morning brief off for a parent who has the mail digest.

Dates taken from mail are not part of the first build: they would come from a separate job on the mail agent (G015, wave C), and how that job hands dates to the brief without passing email text into the parent's main agent still has to be designed. Until then the school deadlines in the week-ahead are rows a parent typed or confirmed (F010).
The National Weather Service forecast reaches seven days ahead, so the Sunday 18:00 weather outlook covers the coming week and no further.

Google's Gemini app can already send a scheduled daily digest of a person's own Google calendar, to-do list and email (being rolled out gradually to personal accounts, up to ten active actions). What Happy's brief adds is the family's own layer: who drives, what to pack from the routines table, the forecast for home, silence on an unremarkable day, and arrival in the iMessage thread.

A mute or a vacation pause (G001) is dependable only for a job that reads the paused-until row in the household store before it writes. The week-ahead and morning legs hold that tool; the evening brief as specified does not, so either add the store read to its tool list or accept that its pause rests on G001's best-effort delivery hook.
unverified: The [T]/[S] driver tag is a family habit the brief depends on, not a product feature; no source can vouch that both adults will keep it up.
gog is not installed, so its flags were checked only against its website, not a binary.
The deadlines input (home-store rows or a sheet) does not exist yet; its shape is a design choice, not a sourced fact.

The catalog passes `home-store__*` in `--tools`; the installed docs document the `<server>__<tool>` prefix only for MCP servers, and home-store is planned as a native plugin, so that glob is untested.
That the NWS forecast endpoints carry no sunrise or sunset field: the opened documentation page does not list one, absence was not proven.
The weather plugin's current fields (12-hour periods, alerts without id, no sunset) were read in ~/src/happy-config/plugins/home-weather/nws.js, which is not one of the two citable source kinds.
safety: Each brief job holds only the weather tool and the read-only calendar tool (plus the household store on the week-ahead and morning legs), has no web tool, and sends its one text only to its own parent. Calendar text can be written by people outside the family (an invitation, a subscribed feed), so it is outside content (see F009); the job's only way out is that one text to its own parent.

name: Dates into reminders and the family calendar after a yes (typed request, flyer photo or PDF)
description: After reading a flyer, slip or schedule, or on a typed request, Happy lists the dates it found, each spelled out in full, and offers reminders or family-calendar entries; nothing is written until the parent says yes. Reminders come first and need no new tool; the calendar entry is a separate, higher-risk step: a write to the family calendar with no invitees after an explicit approve, or a tap-to-add calendar file if a test shows the iPhone offers to add one from Messages.
example: Jordan sends a photo of the soccer season schedule. Happy replies with the eight game dates it read, flags one with no start time, and asks whether to set a reminder the evening before each and to put the games on the family calendar. Nothing is written until she answers.
how: Part 1, proposals (F011): a prompt-level standing order on the parent's own agent, on top of photo and PDF reading (F002) and reminders (F007); a plain conversational proposal, not `ask_user`. Optionally the bundled `llm-task` plugin returns the dates as a schema-checked list (enable the plugin, add it with `tools.alsoAllow`, list both custom model ids in `llm.allowedCompletionModels`, keep `allowModelOverride` false). Part 2, calendar write (F010): an in-house write MCP wrapping `gog calendar create` with its own write token; a `before_tool_call` hook returns `requireApproval` (10-minute cap) and rejects attendees, and the wrapper leaves delete out. A small plugin that emits an .ics attachment is built only if the tap-to-add test passes on both parents' phones.
caveats: Dates read from a photo can be wrong (a missing year, two children on one sheet, a blurry corner), so every proposal spells each date out in full and nothing is written until the parent says yes.
Until the calendar write is built the offer is reminders only; that part needs only photo and PDF reading (F002) and reminders (F007).

The yes before a reminder is a prompt rule; the approval before a calendar write is enforced by the hook. On iMessage that makes a calendar write two steps: the yes to the proposal, then a typed /approve line carrying the request's id, within ten minutes.

The tap-to-add calendar file is unconfirmed: the one report found is of a calendar file that came through Gmail and opened in Files on iOS 18 with no option to add it, so it is tested on both parents' phones before anything is built for it.
For one event on a poster a recent iPhone can already offer to add it from the camera; Happy's part is a sheet with many dates, a PDF, a day-before reminder and the calendar both parents share.
Typing /approve in iMessage Basic mode to resolve the approval was not tested end to end.
The calendar write applies only if the calendar decision lands on Google, and neither the write wrapper nor the calendar-file plugin exists yet.

A list of school deadlines or a season schedule is one more dated document: rows are stored (F031) only after a yes, and the week-ahead brief (F014) reads open school deadlines from there. A lunch menu can be read and asked about like any other photo, but no brief reads stored menu rows, and Happy is never the allergy authority.

Plugin approvals are asked once per tool call, the approval text is capped at 512 characters, and a prompt also offers 'allow always' unless the hook leaves it out. A season schedule is many events, so the write tool should take the whole confirmed list in one call, the approval text should give the count and the date range instead of every row, and the hook should offer only allow-once and deny.
corrections: A 9 Oct note says gog has no delete command. That holds only for the bundled skill text; the gog command index (gogcli.sh/commands) lists gog calendar delete, and gog calendar create accepts --attendees and --send-updates, so the write wrapper must leave delete out and strip those flags itself.

Catalog JSON 'needs' relies on ask_user for the confirmation. ask-user.md:181 says not to use it to confirm a plan, and its wait is clamped to one hour at most (ask-user.md:116-117). The Markdown already switches to a plain proposal.
unverified: That Messages on iPhone offers to add an event when an .ics attachment is tapped. Apple's guide documents .ics import from Mail and by link, and its page body could not be read by the fetch tool. One iOS 18 user on Apple's forum (discussions.apple.com/thread/255997328) reports a calendar file, received through Gmail and opened in the Files app, with no option to add it to Calendar, and a 2022 developer blog post (vadosware.io/post/how-to-import-or-open-ics-files-in-icalendar/) says only Mail and Safari offer to add one; neither covers Messages. Test on both parents' phones before building step 1; if it fails, go straight to the approved write, or try the same file by email to the asker once mailout (F049) exists.
That an .ics file passes OpenClaw's outbound media checks on iMessage (reference/rich-output-protocol.md:22) was not tested.
The in-house .ics generator plugin and the write wrapper do not exist yet.

Typing /approve in iMessage Basic mode to resolve a plugin approval was not tested end to end; the docs say channels without interactive controls fall back to plain-text /approve (exec-approvals-advanced.md:299).
Date extraction accuracy on real flyers (missing years, two children, blurry photos) has not been measured.
The calendar half has not been assessed end to end, because the write wrapper and its approval hook are not built; the reminder half needs only F002 and F007.

Which iPhones the parents carry: MacRumors' guide lists Visual Intelligence for the iPhone 16 family. Apple's own iPhone guide page for the feature returned only its menu in this review, so the phone-side claim rests on MacRumors and iPhone Life.
Whether llm-task runs with a truly empty tool surface on Happy's OpenAI provider route; the doc says the Agents API runtime may keep built-in helpers.
safety: The riskier part is the calendar write: it changes the shared family calendar, so it gets its own token, an approval enforced by a hook that fails closed, no invitees and no delete. Proposals and reminders stay on the parent's own agent and reach only the asker. Flyer text is outside content, so every write waits for a yes.

name: Happy in the parents' group chat: answers when named, and one place for shared announcements
description: Happy joins a three-way iMessage group with both parents and answers when addressed by name. In version 1 the group helper answers from weather and web search only: it keeps no memory and has no calendar or list tools, and passing a message on stays with family delivery (G009). The same chat becomes the one delivery target for announcements meant for both parents, so a watcher needs one job instead of one per parent.
example: In the parents' group Jordan writes: 'Happy, will it rain on Saturday afternoon?' and both parents see the answer. Later a storm-alert text from the weather watcher (F018) arrives once, in the same group, instead of once per parent.
how: groupPolicy allowlist with groupAllowFrom and a groups[chat_id] entry; bindings[] with peer kind group routes it to a stateless family-group agent; mention gating uses the agent name; `channels.imessage.historyLimit: 0`, so that group messages the helper skipped are not handed to it the next time it is named.
caveats: The roadmap's M1 milestone and its S1 channel-isolation baseline keep iMessage groups disabled. This entry re-opens them for one registered chat, with a sender allowlist and mention gating, so it is a change to that baseline for Tony to approve. OpenClaw's security guide calls a private room whose members you trust (team, family or friends) a normal deployment (gateway/security/access-control.md:29).

In Basic mode Happy can read and reply in a group but has no group actions such as renaming it or adding people (private-api.md:29), so a parent creates the group from a phone and Tony reads its chat id with imsg chats.
Both parents see every answer given in the group, so nothing from one parent's memory or mail belongs there; the group helper holds none.

A group that answers only when named still keeps the messages it skipped and adds them as context the next time Happy is named (channels/groups.md:547); the default window is 50 messages. Left on, what the two parents write to each other in the group would reach the cloud model in the same turn as web search results. The group history limit is therefore set to 0 (config-channels/mention-gating-and-history.md:61), so the helper sees only the message that names it.
corrections: Catalog JSON description includes a 'tell everyone dinner is at 6:30' relay and gives the group agent calendar and list tools. Neither exists on the installed stack; the Markdown already moves the relay to G009 and limits version 1 to weather and search.
unverified: Receiving and replying in a three-person group in Basic mode has not been tried live on this Mac; the docs warn that some multi-person threads arrive flagged as non-group unless the chat id is registered (access-control.md:152-153).
Whether a voice memo in the group can satisfy the mention gate on iMessage is not documented (audio.md:286 defers to channel docs).
The numeric chat id is unknown until the group is created and read with imsg chats.

That a history limit of 0 on the iMessage channel stops skipped group messages reaching the helper has not been tried on this Mac; the docs describe the window for all channels and show the key in the iMessage example config (config-channels/personal-messaging.md:172).
safety: The group helper is a separate agent with no memory tools and no calendar, list or mail tools, so nothing held by one parent's own agent can surface in front of the other. Only the two parents' handles pass the group sender allowlist, only the one registered chat is admitted, and Happy answers only when it is named. By default a group that answers only when named keeps up to 50 skipped messages and hands them to the helper the next time it is named, which would put the parents' own conversation in the same turn as web search results; the group history limit is set to 0 so that the helper sees only the message that names it. Web search results are outside content, and the helper can reply only in this group.

name: Two-parent calendar conflict watch
description: When a kid's event on the family calendar in the next 14 days falls at a time when both parents' own calendars show busy, both parents get one line naming the event and the time, once, with an optional who-covers question. Which family-calendar events count has to be a written rule (for example a tag on events that need a driver); without one the watch also flags overlaps that are no problem. Happy only reports; it moves and declines nothing.
example: Trigger: Tony accepts a Thursday 16:00 meeting; Jordan already has the dentist then, and practice is on the family calendar at the same time. Both get: 'Thursday 16:00: both of you show busy during practice. Who covers?'
how: A zero-model command job (`--command-argv`) every few hours, inside the allowed hours only, runs a host script under the happy user: `gog calendar conflicts` (or `freebusy`) across the shared family calendar and the two parents' calendars, compares against a seen-id state file, and prints `NO_REPLY` when nothing is new. To keep each parent's data separate, the script uses one read-only credential that sees the family calendar in full and each parent's own calendar as free/busy only (Google's 'See only free/busy (hide details)' share), so the message names the family-calendar event and says only 'busy' for personal ones. The docs show a single `--to` target per job, so plan one job per parent or the parents' group chat once F006 exists; the follow-up question reuses the ask-and-relay step of G009.
depends_on: F009 read-only calendar on the Google path (decision 4)
gog installed
G009 family delivery, ask-and-relay step (only for the follow-up question)
each parent shares their own calendar with the reading account as free/busy only
F006 parents' group chat, only if one job should reach both parents
caveats: Only applies if the calendar decision lands on Google; the iCloud path would need a different overlap script.
An overlap is not always a problem (both parents at the same recital). Without a rule such as 'kid event with no driver tag' it will cry wolf.
Happy reports; it does not move or decline anything.
Whether phone calendars already warn about cross-person overlaps was not checked; if they do not, this is a gap the phone leaves open.

The notification policy (G001) drops a text sent outside the allowed hours or over the daily cap instead of holding it, and by then the script has recorded the overlap as seen. So the job runs only inside the allowed hours. Timing does not cover the daily cap: a line dropped because the day's cap was reached is lost the same way, since the script cannot tell that its text was cancelled, so this watch's line either sits in a class the cap lets through or that loss is accepted and written into the job's charter.
safety: No model call, so text in event titles cannot steer anything. The calendar grant is read-only. Personal calendars are read as free/busy only, so one parent's private event titles are not shown to the other; only shared family-calendar titles appear, the same exposure as the evening brief. The message goes only to the two parents.
unverified: Flags and JSON output of `gog calendar conflicts`: gog is not installed, only its command list page was read.
How Ohai's conflict check behaves in use; its feature page says it scans connected calendars, flags overlapping events and offers to reschedule, which goes further than Happy's report-only line.
Whether `gog calendar conflicts` works on calendars shared as free/busy only.

That phone calendars give no cross-person overlap warning: a web search in round 3 found no Google or Apple help page describing one, only forum posts, so it is still not settled by an official source.
Whether one job can announce to two recipients; the docs' examples show a single `--to` target.

Where each parent's work meetings live. The card's example turns on a work meeting; an employer's Google calendar can be shared outside the organisation only up to the level its administrator sets (Google's admin page 'Set Google Calendar sharing options', knowledge.workspace.google.com/admin/calendar/set-google-calendar-sharing-options, lists 'Only free/busy information' as the narrowest choice), and a work calendar that is not on Google cannot be read by gog at all.

name: Trip and outing planner (day trip, weekend, multi-day)
description: 'Plan Saturday for us, kids 8 and 10, rain likely' returns two options with opening hours, the weather and links, and admission prices where a page could be read. A longer plan (a weekend or several days) can be emailed to the asker; hotels and transport come as links, not prices. For a trip abroad with the children the plan ends with a paperwork line: whether the passports cover the dates, and a pointer to the official page on the consent letter advised when a child travels with only one parent or without either parent. An optional Friday 16:00 job sends a 'this weekend near us' text built the same way. The parents book.
example: Jordan texts: 'Plan Saturday for us, kids 8 and 10, rain likely.' Happy answers 'on it', then sends two options, one indoors and one outdoors with a rain fallback, each with opening hours, Saturday's forecast, a link, and the admission price where the venue's page showed one.
how: One research sub-agent run via `sessions_spawn` with `runTimeoutSeconds`, composing `web_fetch`, the place lookup and `home_weather`; calendar free time crosses as date ranges only; the Friday 16:00 job reuses it. The place lookup is a tool on the research agent and one of two connections to Google's place data: the `goplaces` command that OpenClaw bundles a skill for, wrapped as a host-side stdio MCP with `GOOGLE_PLACES_API_KEY` and the home coordinates held in the wrapper, or Google's hosted Maps server (Grounding Lite), which the roadmap names. For a trip abroad the parent's own agent, not research, adds the paperwork line from the renewals table (F063) and fixed official links; passport dates and names are never handed to research.
caveats: Happy books and pays for nothing: the plan ends in links and the parents book.
Prices are best effort. Plain page reads fail on many booking, hotel and transport sites, so those come as links, and an admission price appears only when a page that could be read showed it.

The pieces arrive at different times: opening hours and ratings need the place lookup (formerly F021, now part of this entry and not built), an hour-by-hour rain line needs the weather upgrade (F083), the emailed long version needs mailout (F049) and the passport line needs the renewals table (F063). Until then the plan is built from web pages and the half-day forecast and comes back as a text.
Drive time is not part of the plan unless a route lookup is added with the place lookup.
Only ages, a place, a distance and free dates as ranges are meant to reach the research agent; that is an instruction to the parent's agent, not an enforced limit.

The paperwork line is a pointer, not a ruling. USAGov's page on travel documents for children (usa.gov/travel-documents-children) covers trips abroad and says a consent letter, preferably notarised, should come from the other parent when a child travels with one parent, and from both when the child travels with a guardian or alone. Entry rules differ by country and airline, and Happy certifies nothing.

A general assistant such as Gemini already drafts an itinerary from a typed prompt, as the Google post behind this card shows. Happy's version saves retyping the family's ages, free dates and home weather, and adds the paperwork line.

The roadmap's research milestone names Google's hosted Maps server (Grounding Lite) for place data, and OpenClaw bundles a skill for the goplaces command instead. Both read Google's place data and both need billing switched on, so one is chosen before building. Google's page says the hosted server's place search returns an AI-generated summary with place ids and Maps links and does not mention opening hours, so check first that it can answer 'is it open now?'.
For a one-off 'is it open now?' the maps app on a parent's phone is quicker and has live traffic. The place lookup is here as data for the plan, not as a separate thing to ask Happy.
corrections: Drive time was dropped from the 9 Oct wording because goplaces was thought to lack it; upstream goplaces `directions` or Grounding Lite `compute_routes` can supply it.
unverified: Hotel and train price snapshots: no opened source shows these sites are readable logged-out; expect links instead of prices.
The weather plugin returns 12-hour periods today (read in ~/src/happy-config, not citable), so an hourly rain window needs the plugin change in F083.
The emailed long version depends on the mailout server (F049), not built.
Current Places and Routes prices and free allowances were not read.
goplaces is not installed, so its flags were checked against the bundled skill and the upstream README only.
Whether Grounding Lite is generally available or a preview: Google's page does not label it.
safety: The research agent holds no family data: it is given ages, a place, a distance and free dates as ranges only (a prompt rule on the parent's agent, not an enforced limit), and it has no payment or booking tool. The paperwork line for a trip abroad uses passport dates and names, so the parent's own agent writes it and none of it is handed to research. Answers go only to the asking parent. The Google key and the home coordinates sit in the host-side wrapper, not in the prompt, and every place query goes to Google.

name: Model-free watchers on public sources: storm alerts for home, moved games and changed pages, matched recalls
description: Scripts with no model check public sources on a schedule and text a parent once when something new matters: a winter storm, wind, flood or freeze alert for home (with a chore checklist and, on a school night, a line to watch for the school's own notice), a practice or game that moved or a registered site that posted something new, or a product, food or medicine recall that matches what the family owns. Each watch is its own switch that Tony sets up; Happy does not know whether school is closed.
example: Trigger: the Saturday game's start time changes in the team's feed. Text: 'Soccer Saturday moved from 9:00 to 10:30, same field.'
how: All are operator-created host command jobs (`--command-argv`) with no model call: a script fetches a public source, keeps seen ids in a state file and prints one templated line or `NO_REPLY`. Weather (F018): `nws-alerts.mjs` every 30 minutes polls the National Weather Service active-alerts feed for the home point and dedups on the alert id. Schedules and pages (F029, SRC-09): `ics-watch.mjs`, hourly in season, reads a team's subscription link and reports changed events in the next seven days; `watch-page.mjs` every 6 hours uses a site's feed when there is one, otherwise a plain https GET and a text hash. Recalls (SRC-03, SRC-04): `cpsc-recalls.mjs` daily and `fda-recalls.mjs` twice a day, matched locally against owned-item, allergen, staples and medicine keyword lists. The schedule, page and recall jobs are timed inside the allowed hours of the notification policy (G001); only the storm-alert job runs round the clock.
caveats: A parent cannot start a watch from chat: command jobs are created by the operator, so each new watch is a request to Tony.

None of these gives earlier notice than the source's own service: Apple's Weather app can notify about government alerts once that is switched on, the team app's push is faster for a same-day change, and both recall agencies offer their own sign-ups; Happy adds the match, the school-night line and one text to both parents.
Happy is down in a power cut or a network outage and FDA's own list does not carry every recall, so silence from a watch is never an all-clear and the phones' emergency alerts stay on.
With a shared state file the second parent's job finds nothing new and stays silent, so each parent's job keeps its own file or one job delivers to the parents' group chat.

Command jobs run on the Gateway host as the happy user, outside the sandbox, agent tool policy and OpenClaw's fetch guardrails, so the scripts check each address themselves (https, public host) and are reviewed like the rest of the config repo.
A team's subscription link is a bearer secret, so it sits in a file only the happy user can read and stays out of family.json5 if that file is committed.
A hash watch on a school or town page can fire on changes that do not matter, pages that need JavaScript are out of reach, and many school portals publish no feed.

The recall match is only as good as the family's lists (substring matching gives false positives and misses unlisted items), and meat and poultry recalls and cars are not covered; parents add VINs and car seats to NHTSA's own app.

The notification policy (G001) drops a text sent outside the allowed hours or over the daily cap instead of holding it, and by then the script has recorded the item as seen, so a change found at night would never be told. The schedule, page and recall scripts therefore run only inside the allowed hours. The storm alert goes in G001's urgent class, which passes quiet hours, so a storm text can arrive in the night; if that is not wanted, the storm job can be timed inside the allowed hours as well, once a test shows that an alert issued overnight is still in the active-alerts feed at the first morning run. Timing does not cover the daily cap: a watcher text dropped because the day's cap was reached is lost the same way, since the script cannot tell that its text was cancelled, so watcher texts either sit in a class the cap lets through or that loss is accepted and written into each job's charter.
corrections: The catalog's needs used `--once` and the verifier said no CLI flag exists (JSON or Control UI only); the installed CLI source defines `--trigger-once`.
unverified: That an NWS update to an existing alert arrives under a new id pointing back through `references`: the fields were seen, their semantics were not read, so the dedup rule needs a test.
The current weather plugin returns alerts without an id (read in ~/src/happy-config, not a citable source kind), which is why the script calls the API directly.
Which alert types the Weather app's severe-weather notification covers: Apple's pages say government-issued severe weather alerts without listing them.
Which of the family's school, town and camp sites publish a feed, and which registration pages can be read without JavaScript.
The five-watchers-per-person cap is a convention; nothing enforces it.
Which agent's session transcript receives the mirrored announce line of a command job; check by reading the transcript after the first run, and keep the line short and templated.
GameChanger's exact rules on who can sync practices versus games.
How quickly each service's .ics link itself reflects a change (only the downstream calendar lag is documented).
Rate limits or terms for polling the subscription links hourly.
Formal terms of use or rate limit for the recall web service (the page read gives none).
Documentation for the RecallDateStart parameter (it is not on the API information page read; it is confirmed only by the live response).
The USDA FSIS recall API (endpoint, fields, terms): the page returned 403.
Whether the FDA RSS feed has a documented polling limit.
safety: No model reads any feed, page or recall: each script prints a fixed line with outside titles stripped and capped, and only the official or registered link. Requests go only to addresses Tony registered, and nothing about the family is sent out. Team schedules say where the kids will be, so they stay on the host and go only to pinned parent handles.

name: Meals to the grocery list: recipe links, a recipe box and a Sunday dinner plan
description: Text a recipe link and get the ingredient list and the steps, scaled to the number of people, with an offer to add the ingredients to the shared grocery list and to save the recipe. On Sunday afternoon the parent who cooks gets five dinner ideas drawn from the saved recipes and fitted to the week's calendar and allergies; a reply swaps a night or adds a dinner's ingredients to the list.
example: A parent texts: '<recipe link> What do I need for this for six people?' Or the Sunday trigger: five dinner ideas arrive and the cook replies 'swap Wednesday'.
how: Recipe link (WEB-11): the parent's own agent hands the URL to the research agent with `sessions_spawn`; research fetches the page with `web_fetch`, makes one `llm-task` call with a small schema (title, yield, ingredients, steps, source link) and returns it. The parent's agent scales quantities, proposes items for the shared grocery list (F030), written only after a yes, and after a yes saves the recipe to the recipe box: a page in the family vault (F043, its memory-wiki step, written with `wiki_apply`). Recipe text does not go into the household store (F031), whose rows are meant to stay short and typed. Sunday plan (F033): an isolated scheduled job on the parent's agent reads the saved recipes and the calendar and saves the plan, as recipe titles against days, for the main session to use when the parent replies; nothing is ordered. Pages plain fetch cannot read fall back to the research browser and the summarize wrapper (F020).
caveats: The recipe box starts empty; a recipe gets in when a parent sends a link and says yes to saving it.
The fetch returns readable article text, not the page's embedded recipe data, so the model parses ingredients from prose and can drop a line; the source link is always included.
Some recipe sites sit behind bot walls or paywalls and return nothing; Happy says so instead of guessing.
The phone's reader view and recipe-keeper apps already clean up a recipe page; the added value is the hand-off to the shared grocery list and a plan fitted to the family calendar.
Happy does not know what is in the kitchen, so it offers the whole ingredient list and the parent strikes what they have.
Scaling quantities is arithmetic done by a language model: fine for a stew, worth a second look for baking.
The reading part works the day the research agent exists; the grocery hand-off waits on the Reminders bridge (F030) and the Sunday plan on the calendar connection (F009), and neither exists yet.
The schema fixes the shape of what research returns, not its content, and nothing in the platform forces that check to run.

The allergy fit is the model reading the family's allergy notes against each recipe's ingredient list. It can miss an allergen that sits inside an ingredient, so Happy is never the allergy authority and the cook still checks ingredients and labels.

A saved recipe is text lifted from a web page, and the Sunday job and both parents' agents read it back later, so it is a place where an instruction hidden in a page could persist.
